constructs.label: `Event::dispatch()` (an event object)
constructs.note: The listener is a class, so the build compiles it (the event classes + the listeners, dist/src/classes.generated.mjs). The dispatch is synchronous, like Laravel's.

constructs.label: `Gate::authorize()`
constructs.note: It throws an AuthorizationException (a 403). The edge renders the app's own `resources/views/errors/403.blade.php` when it exists (the same as every other status error), so the working path is `Gate::allows()` + `abort(403)`.

constructs.label: `Gate::before()`

constructs.label: `Mail::to()->send()`
constructs.note: A mailable is a class: the build compiles it (the dump takes the app's Mail classes, the class compiler emits the class and the kernel's Mailable base carries Laravel's fluent surface) and the mailer sends the payload Laravel sends - the recipients, the subject and the rendered view (the mailable's data goes into the view). The byte-for-byte proof is the shadow: the PHP oracle captures Laravel's `MessageSent` event (the from/to/cc/bcc/replyTo/subject/html/text) and the harness compares those fields with the kernel mailer's outbox - all 8 fields are identical, the log line is not compared. The methods the kernel mailer does not implement (raw, html, queue, later) fail loud.

constructs.label: `Mail::send()` (a view name)
constructs.note: Laravel's Mailer::send() has two shapes: a Mailable INSTANCE (it is sent as it is) and a VIEW NAME (Laravel renders the view with the data and sends THAT - the route answers 200 and the mail goes out). The edge has only the first shape: the compiled mailer carries a payload (a compiled Mailable, or an object with to/subject/html), so a view name throws at request time ("mail(): the message is not a payload") and the route answers 500 - the build refuses the view shape instead of shipping a route that 500s where Laravel sends the mail. A mailable still compiles (`Mail::send(new OrderMail())` and `Mail::to($user)->send(new OrderMail())`); a dynamic first argument is NOT refused (it can hold a mailable and the build cannot prove which it is - refusing it would refuse a legal send).
constructs.reason: a view name is not a payload at the edge

constructs.label: `Queue::push()`
constructs.note: The job would never run at the edge: the worker has no queue handler, so nothing consumes the queue binding, and the binding carries a JSON body, not a PHP job. The paths that work: a Cloudflare Queues binding with a consumer you write (a limited version is on the Workers free plan; the paid plan charges per operation), or a D1 table the cron trigger reads (a port handler writes the row - the edge has no producer for it). The job class is not compiled either: the class compiler compiles the events, the listeners and the injected services - a job is none of them. In Laravel the job is queued (or run inline by the sync driver) and the route answers 200.
constructs.reason: the job would never run at the edge

constructs.label: `Job::dispatch()` on a compiled job class
constructs.note: A job class the build compiles (app/Jobs): `dispatch()` writes a row into the D1 `lw_jobs` table and the CRON TRIGGER drains it, so the job runs after the response (Laravel's `database` driver). The build refuses the push when the worker has no cron trigger - the job would never run. The `Queue` FACADE (`Queue::push`) stays refused: it takes a class-name string the edge cannot resolve to a compiled class.

constructs.label: `Storage::disk()` (the default disk)
constructs.note: The default disk is the compiled object store (the D1 blob store, or R2 when bound).

constructs.label: `Storage::disk()` (a named disk)
constructs.note: A named disk needs a bucket of its own (R2 asks for a credit card); the compiled rung has one store.
constructs.reason: has ONE object store

constructs.label: `Cache::tags()`
constructs.note: The compiled cache store is the D1 `database` store, which has no tags: in Laravel this route 500s with BadMethodCallException("This cache store does not support tagging."); the build refuses the route before it ships (stricter than Laravel, not a parity), and a taggable store (redis/memcached) is not compiled.
constructs.reason: the compiled cache store is the D1 `database` store

constructs.label: Blade `@extends` (a layout)
constructs.note: The sections travel to the layout (the shadow harness proves the bytes).

constructs.label: `Model::paginate()`
constructs.note: The LengthAwarePaginator (the items, the total, the pages, the URLs) + the pagination links (the framework's `pagination::tailwind` view is compiled at build time).

constructs.label: The translation helper (`__()`)
constructs.note: The strings are dumped at build time (the app's lang/ files + the framework's fallback); the place-holders are replaced like Laravel does.

constructs.label: A PHP cast (`(string) $x`)
constructs.note: The scalar casts with PHP's own semantics: (string), (int), (bool), (float).

constructs.label: Route-model binding (a typed param)
constructs.note: The model comes from the route segment (Laravel's implicit binding); a missing model is a 404.

constructs.label: Eloquent relations (`$post->comments()`)
constructs.note: A relation is not compiled: the build stops (LW003). The eager loading (`with()`) is not compiled at the edge either - the relations are a planned milestone (M64), so a route that reads one needs a port handler until then.
constructs.reason: is not compiled (an Eloquent relation?)

constructs.label: File upload (`$request->file()`)
constructs.note: The multipart body is parsed at the edge: the file object carries the metadata (the name, the type the browser declared, the size) and the store (the app's default disk). Byte-proven by the shadow harness.

constructs.label: The upload is stored (`$file->storeAs()`)
constructs.note: The object store (the D1 blob store on the free plan, R2 with a bucket of its own): the path is the disk-relative one Laravel returns (trim($path.'/'.$name, '/')).

constructs.label: The upload is stored under a random name (`$file->store()`)
constructs.note: The name is a random hash (Str::random(40)) + the extension; the extension comes from the type the browser declared (Laravel sniffs the content with finfo).

constructs.label: The content type of the upload (`$file->getMimeType()`)
constructs.note: The content type is read from the file's bytes (finfo): the edge cannot sniff the content like PHP does, so the build stops (LW003).
constructs.reason: it reads the file's content type (finfo)

constructs.label: A `mimes` rule on an upload
constructs.note: The `mimes` rule compares the extension the content sniffs (finfo): the edge has only the type the browser declared, so the build stops (LW002) instead of answering differently.
constructs.reason: it reads the file's *content* type (finfo)

constructs.label: An `image`/`dimensions` rule on an upload
constructs.note: `image` and `dimensions` are getimagesize(), a HEADER read (ValidatesAttributes::validateImage/validateDimensions): the edge reads the same header (kernel/image.mjs) and applies the same named checks, so the verdict is Laravel's. The finfo rules (`mimes`, `mimetypes`) stay refused.

constructs.label: The files bag as a method (`$request->files()`)
constructs.note: In Laravel `$request->files` is a property (Symfony's FileBag), not a method: the build stops (LW002) and points at `$request->file()` / `$request->allFiles()`.
constructs.reason: in Laravel it is a property (Symfony's FileBag), not a method

constructs.label: An `OPTIONS` route
constructs.note: The compiled side answers Laravel's automatic OPTIONS response (200 + the Allow header - byte-proven); a CORS config makes the build skip the route.

constructs.label: A relation read as a property (`$post->comments`)
constructs.note: A relation (or an accessor) read as a property is not compiled: the build stops (LW003). It used to answer null - a wrong answer, silently.
constructs.reason: is not compiled (a relation or an accessor?)

constructs.label: A rule object (`Rule::file()->max()`)
constructs.note: A rule object in a CONTROLLER's validate() call is a class: the compiler cannot evaluate it at build time (the rules live in the controller's source), so the rule would be silently ignored and the validation would differ. The build stops and names what it would take. (In a FormRequest the dump normalizes the object to its string form - the row below.)
constructs.reason: a rule object

constructs.label: A rule object in a FormRequest
constructs.note: The FormRequest dump reads the rules Laravel itself builds and NORMALIZES a rule object to its string form (Laravel hands the validator the object and the validator reads that string): `Rule::in(['a','b'])` becomes `in:"a","b"` - which the kernel parses exactly like Laravel (M61a). A CONDITIONAL rule object is refused (the row below).

constructs.label: A conditional rule object in a FormRequest
constructs.note: A conditional rule object (`Rule::requiredIf(true)`, `Rule::when(...)`) is refused: its string form is the CONDITION evaluated at build time (`RequiredIf::__toString()` returns 'required' or ''), so the edge would bake the build-time branch into the rule - a request Laravel accepts could be rejected (or the other way round). The dump stops with that reason (LW003).

constructs.label: `prepareForValidation()` (overridden)
constructs.note: The hook is COMPILED: the build compiles the FormRequest class (the dump registers it), the compiled handler runs the hook BEFORE the validation (Laravel's order - ValidatesWhenResolvedTrait::validateResolved), and the input the hook prepares is what the rules see. The compiled class extends the kernel's `kernel/form-request.mjs` - the request surface the hook uses (merge(), input(), all()).

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides `after()` / `validationData()` / `passedValidation()`
constructs.note: All three hooks run in the compiled lifecycle, in Laravel's order: `validationData()` is the data source, `after()` registers its RETURN VALUE as a validator callback, and `passedValidation()` runs after the rules pass. Proven by the shadow (`POST /hooked-request-demo` 422/422 for the `after()` refusal and 200/200 carrying the `passedValidation` marker).

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides `withValidator()`
constructs.note: Laravel calls the hook with the validator right after it is built (`Foundation/Http/FormRequest.php:110`), so the app's custom messages and its `after()` callbacks run. The compiled class carries the hook and the lifecycle calls it with the kernel's validator, in Laravel's order. Proven by the shadow (`POST /hooked-request-demo` 422/422 byte-identical when `withValidator()` refuses the flag) and by the compiled handler's `hooks: [...]` list.

constructs.label: A listener that injects a service
constructs.class_php:
<?php
namespace App\Listeners;

use App\Events\PostPublished;
use App\Services\Mailer;

class L
{
    public function __construct(private Mailer $mailer)
    {
    }

    public function handle(PostPublished $event): void
    {
        $this->mailer->send($event);
    }
}
constructs.note: A service the build does not compile: the edge has no container and no file for it, so the constructor dependency is a build error (the build names the class). A service the build DOES compile is injected (the edge builds it) and a framework service is adapted (the worker hands the live one down).
constructs.reason: the build does not compile it

constructs.label: an API resource (`return new PostResource($post)`)
constructs.note: The controller answers a JsonResource; the Router's prepareResponse() wraps it in a ResourceResponse - `{"data": {...}, ...with($request)}` (JsonResource::toArray + the `$wrap` key, ResourceResponse.php:31-52). The app declares only toArray()/with(); the rest is the kernel base. Byte-proven by the shadow (`GET /resource-demo` identical) and by compiler/tests/resource-class.test.mjs; the audit probes it as a controller fragment with the class registry the build passes. A body that needs an await fails loud (the response path is synchronous).

constructs.label: A FormRequest that overrides `validator()`
constructs.note: Laravel asks the app's own factory for the validator (`FormRequest::getValidatorInstance()`), so an override decides the rules, the messages and the factory itself. The edge has ONE validator factory, so the dump refuses the class (LW003, `tools/formrequest-dump.php`) and the build stops instead of validating with different rules than Laravel.
